current_answer: Job ads may change before a worker loses a job. A U.S. preprint scores 9.37 million online postings and finds that, after mid-2023, both shifts in which roles were advertised and changes in listed tasks within comparable job categories contributed to a decline in measured GenAI exposure. That is a change in vacancy text, not proof AI caused employers to redesign jobs or cut staff. Separate studies still warn of weaker junior entry in specific samples, while a broad U.S. tracker finds no clear economy-wide AI jobs footprint. The startup evidence also shows why more new firms need not mean more startup jobs. No study here predicts an individual worker’s outcome.

catalogue_card.question: Are job ads changing before jobs disappear?
catalogue_card.text: A U.S. study finds changing task descriptions within comparable advertised roles. It measures AI-exposure scores in ads, not AI-caused layoffs or completed hires.

summary: U.S. posting data show that both the mix of advertised roles and listed tasks within comparable categories changed as measured GenAI exposure fell after mid-2023.
The posting result does not establish that employers adopted AI, redesigned the same job or cut workers; its exposure trend began before ChatGPT.
Narrow junior-entry warnings and a broad U.S. no-clear-footprint result still use different outcomes. Startup entry is not equivalent to net jobs or similar-pay opportunities.
uncertainty: The new posting study scores vacancy text with LLMs; realized job tasks and worker outcomes are not observed.
Within-group changes do not track the same firm or job over time. The early-2022 exposure peak limits AI attribution.
Existing hiring and startup studies cover different populations and cannot predict individual risk.
freshness_note: Checked 5 October 2026. Added full-paper evidence that AI-exposure scores in U.S. job ads move through both posting mix and within-category task text, without a causal or worker-outcome claim.
